newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ASEAN - U.S. business opposes unilateral sanctions.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN - U.S. business opposes unilateral sanctions.

text.p: Business leaders from the United States and Southeast Asia on Thursday criticised unilateral economic sanctions imposed by Washington as ineffective.

"Unilateral economic sanctions, or the threat of such sanctions, do not achieve the desired improvements in human rights and workers' rights," a wide-ranging position paper by the ASEAN-U.S. Business Council said.

The council, a private group aimed at boosting interest and investment in the region, presented the paper to the ASEAN-U.S. Dialogue of government officials and business leaders who meet annually to discuss security, political and economic issues of mutual interest.
The paper was put to the meeting by Malaysia's Petronas chairman Tan Sri Azizan Zainul Abidin and George David, president of United Technologies Corp of the United States.

David said in a news briefing on Tuesday that sanctions did not work and that United Technologies expected to invest in Burma in the next three or four years despite U.S. threats of sanctions against the Rangoon government over its democracy and human rights records.
He said the best method of change was "involvement and persuasion... instead of subjecting people to isolation".

The position paper strongly supported development of the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA), deregulation of trade and investment, capital market development in the region and extended double taxation treaties.
ASEAN groups Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, the Philippines and Vietnam. Laos and Cambodia are due to join next year, and Burma sometime in the near future.
The paper also said human rights and workers rights issues should be addressed through bilateral and multilateral diplomatic channels.
The U.S. government has said it wanted to raise such issues at the inaugural ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in Singapore in December.
Indonesia's President Suharto echoed ASEAN's feeling when he said in opening an ASEAN economic ministers' meeting in Jakarta on Thursday that the WTO should stick strictly to trade matters.

U.S. delegation member Ernest Bower, president of the U.S.-ASEAN Council for Business and Technology, told reporters at the Batam meeting their concern about sanctions extended to those proposed or imposed against Burma, Cuba and Iran.
"The threat of unilateral economic sanctions in the case of Burma or our sanctions in other countries such as Cuba and Iran could penalise some ASEAN countries," Bower said.
"(This) is probably the most near-term and serious threat to our ability to continue very good relations with ASEAN and other countries around the world," he said.

Bower said ASEAN was irresistible to U.S. business because at the turn of the century it would be a 10-member group with a combined gross domestic product of $1.0 trillion. Two-way trade would be $250 billion in a market of 500 million people.
"We know that shortly after the turn of the century, on current growth rates, ASEAN will overtake Japan as our second largest trading partner," he said.
